back: The state of having a very large supply; a great quantity of something.
extra: The harvest brought an abundance of apples and pears.

back: The state of a thing being rare or in short supply; a lack of enough of something.
extra: Scarcity of fresh water forced the village to ration its use.

back: Enough or good enough for a particular purpose; sufficient.
extra: The food the family stored was adequate for the winter.

back: Open to more than one interpretation; not having one clear meaning.
extra: The instructions were so ambiguous that no one knew what to do.

back: Kind, generous, and caring about the well-being of others.
extra: The benevolent neighbor shared her garden with the whole street.

back: The feeling of being thankful; gratefulness.
extra: She expressed her gratitude with a handwritten note.

back: To allow yourself to enjoy something, especially something you ought to limit.
extra: After hours of studying, he indulged in a slice of chocolate cake.

back: Gentle in strength or degree; not harsh or extreme.
extra: The school has a mild winter when the temperature never falls below freezing.

back: To restore harmony between people; to bring differing views into agreement.
extra: It took weeks before the two friends could reconcile after the argument.

back: Producing powerful, clear, and detailed images in the mind.
extra: The witness gave a vivid description of the car that hit him.

back: To force or oblige someone to do something; to make it impossible not to feel a certain way.
extra: The evidence compelled the jury to reach a guilty verdict.

back: Showing steady, careful effort and hard work; industrious.
extra: A diligent student checks the homework list every single day.

back: The ability to understand and share the feelings of another person.
extra: Empathy helped her see why her classmate was upset.

back: Possible and practical to do easily; can be done successfully.
extra: Building a bridge that long is not feasible without much more funding.

back: Very serious, severe, or causing great sorrow and distress.
extra: The news of the grievous loss made the whole town mourn.

back: Unfriendly; openly opposed or unfriendly to someone.
extra: The strangers were hostile at first until they were shown the camp's rules.

back: The quality of being honest and having strong moral principles.
extra: The judge praised the young man's integrity when he returned the lost wallet.

back: Not large or impressive in size or amount; showing humility and not being boastful.
extra: The scientist is modest about the awards she has won.

back: To formally propose someone for an award, position, or role.
extra: The committee nominated the teacher for the prize of the year.

back: No longer produced or used; out of date; no longer in use.
extra: The old fax machine is obsolete now that everyone uses email.

back: To convince someone to do something or believe something by reasoning or argument.
extra: The mayor tried to persuade the citizens to support the new library.

back: Very deep or intense; having a strong effect; creating a deep sense of something.
extra: The book made a profound impression on every reader in the class.

back: Unwilling and hesitant to do something; not eager or willing to act.
extra: He was reluctant to speak in front of the whole assembly.

back: Spread or placed at random over an area; not kept together in one place.
extra: The scattered seeds took months to grow into a full garden.

back: Very large, great, or impressive in size, amount, or degree.
extra: The crowd gave the player a tremendous applause after the final game.

back: Able to be physically or emotionally hurt easily; defenseless.
extra: The injured deer lay vulnerable beside the road at dawn.

back: Loyalty or firm commitment to a person, group, or cause.
extra: His deep allegiance to his country kept him serving for decades.

back: (of land) not able to produce much or no crops; unproductive and empty.
extra: The barren hillside turned green once the rains finally returned.

back: To think about something in a calm, serious way for a long time; to ponder.
extra: She sat by the window to contemplate her decision about moving.

back: To damage something very badly; to destroy; to cause great distress or shock.
extra: The flood devastated the farmland along the river for years.

back: To add more details to something in order to make it fuller or clearer; to expand on.
extra: The speaker elaborated on each point with concrete examples.

back: Easily broken or damaged; delicate and not able to withstand much shock.
extra: Handle the old porcelain cups with care; they are extremely fragile.

back: A danger or risk; something that might cause harm to a person or place.
extra: Swimming in the stormy sea is a serious hazard for the crew.

back: A reward, reason, or extra benefit given to motivate someone to do something.
extra: The bonus was an incentive for the workers to finish the project early.

back: To put something at risk or in danger; to threaten to harm or spoil.
extra: Skipping breakfast before the exam will jeopardize her concentration.

back: Of the same family; related by blood; similar or kind in kind and character.
extra: The two cousins have kindred interests in music and sports.

back: Done with visible effort or difficulty; hard-earned and not smooth.
extra: The hikers made labored progress up the steep rocky mountain trail.

back: Showing great care and attention to detail; very thorough and exacting.
extra: A meticulous map-maker checked every distance twice before printing.

back: The failure to take proper care in doing something; carelessness or thoughtlessness.
extra: The fire was caused by simple negligence in the kitchen.

back: Willing to follow orders or rules; well-mannered and compliant with what is asked.
extra: The obedient dog sat and waited before taking its treat.

back: Seeming reasonable, probable, or believable; making a good argument for being true.
extra: His explanation for being late was plausible, but the teacher was not sure.

back: To satisfy a thirst or desire; to put out or extinguish a fire or flame completely.
extra: A large glass of cold water quenched her thirst after the long run.

back: A place of safety, shelter, or protection; a place to flee to for safety.
extra: The forest gave the lost hikers a temporary refuge from the rain.

back: To examine or inspect something very carefully and in detail; to look closely for faults.
extra: The judge will scrutinize every page of the long contract before signing.

back: Holding firmly; persisting and not giving up; difficult to remove or shake off.
extra: The tenacious climber refused to give up on the steep cliff face.

back: In the end; finally; as the final result or ultimate outcome.
extra: Ultimately, the team won the championship after a long, hard season.

back: To justify, authorise, or give a good reason for something; to call for something.
extra: No single mistake is enough to warrant expelling a student from school.

back: Great energy, enthusiasm, or passionate dedication in pursuit of something.
extra: The volunteers worked with zeal to rebuild the damaged community hall.

back: To go do small tasks or chores for someone else (buying things, mailing letters, etc.).
extra: My older sister runs errands for our family on Saturday mornings.

back: To ease the tension or awkwardness at the start of a meeting or social gathering; to get a conversation started.
extra: The teacher asked for a short icebreaker to break the ice with the new student.

back: To accept a difficult or unpleasant situation with good humor and without complaining.
extra: She had to bite the bullet and tell her friend the exam results were bad.

front: hit the nail on the head
back: To do or say something exactly right; to be precisely accurate or correct.
extra: His explanation hit the nail on the head about why the experiment failed.

back: In a final, complete, and decisive way; ending something permanently with no repetition.
extra: The council voted to fix the leaking roof once and for all.

back: By a very small amount or margin; almost not; barely enough.
extra: The team lost the game by a hair, with one point to spare.

back: To do something in a quicker or cheaper way, usually reducing quality or safety.
extra: Cutting corners on the construction plan is not allowed on any job site.

back: To tell a secret that was supposed to be kept private; to reveal information too soon.
extra: Don't spill the beans about the surprise party before Friday.

back: To leave or set off on a journey, usually by car or on foot.
extra: We hit the road at dawn to reach the coast before lunch.

back: Something very easy to do; a simple task that requires little effort.
extra: The history quiz was a piece of cake after two weeks of study.

front: A {{c1::concise}} statement says the same thing in fewer words than a long, wordy one.
extra: The manager replaced the ten-line memo with a concise three-line one.

front: A {{c1::generous}} person is happy to give time, money, or help to others without being asked.
extra: He was generous with his time, helping every new student in the club.

front: A {{c1::resilient}} person recovers quickly from difficulties, setbacks, or illness.
extra: The resilient farmer replanted his field after the unexpected frost.

front: An {{c1::inevitable}} result is something that is certain to happen and cannot be avoided.
extra: The players accepted their defeat as inevitable once the star player was injured.

front: A {{c1::skeptical}} person is doubtful or unconvinced about a claim until real evidence is shown.
extra: He was skeptical of the advertisement until he read the full product reviews.

front: A {{c1::tolerant}} person accepts and respects views, habits, or people that differ from their own.
extra: A tolerant community welcomes newcomers with different traditions.

front: To {{c1::verify}} something means to check that it is true, accurate, or valid before accepting it.
extra: The editor verified every statistic in the article before it was published.

front: A {{c1::wary}} person is cautious, watchful, and suspicious of possible danger or harm.
extra: The hikers were wary of the dark tunnel and moved slowly through it.

front: Doing something {{c1::in advance}} means doing it before the time it is needed or expected.
extra: Please register in advance so the organizers can reserve your seat.

front: Being {{c1::in debt}} means owing money to a bank, person, or organization that must be paid back.
extra: The small shop was in debt until the new customer orders arrived.

front: Two people who are {{c1::at odds}} disagree or are in conflict or tension with each other.
extra: The brothers were at odds over which route to take on the hike.

front: Doing something {{c1::on purpose}} means doing it deliberately and intentionally, not by accident.
extra: She was not late by mistake; she went on purpose to watch the sunset first.

front: Trying something {{c1::in vain}} means the effort was made but failed; it was useless or pointless.
extra: All his attempts to convince the jury were in vain.

front: Being {{c1::at a loss}} means not knowing what to say or do in a difficult situation.
extra: When asked to explain the mistake, she stood at a loss for words.

front: To {{c1::keep an eye}} on something means to watch it carefully and stay alert for changes or problems.
extra: Please keep an eye on my bag while I step inside to use the restroom.

front: Helping someone {{c1::in a pinch}} means helping them in a difficult or urgent situation when they need it most.
extra: She always comes in a pinch to lend money or a ride to a friend.

front: Being {{c1::over the moon}} means being extremely happy, pleased, or delighted about something.
extra: The children were over the moon when the zoo announced a new panda exhibit.

front: Something that stays {{c1::under the radar}} is not noticed or detected by other people or authorities.
extra: The quiet inventor developed her idea under the radar of big companies.

front: Arriving {{c1::in the nick of time}} means arriving just before it is too late to be useful.
extra: The bus arrived in the nick of time as the station was about to close.

front: If you {{c1::miss}} the bus, you fail to board it because you were late or it left without you.
extra: I missed the first train and had to wait forty minutes for the next one.

front: To {{c1::throw something together}} means to make or arrange it quickly, without much care for quality.
extra: We threw together a small dinner for the unexpected visitors.
